### On Unreal Engine - The Source Build Version of the Engine

Welcome. In order to package a dedicated server project in Unreal Engine, we need a source build of the engine. What does this mean? Well, when you download Unreal Engine from the Epic Games launcher, you're downloading a precompiled binary version which is smaller and easier to download. The actual source build of the engine is upwards of 200GB. We need that build because the binary distribution of unreal that you get from the Epic Games launcher is not capable of packaging a dedicated server. So in this section, we're going to follow the steps to download Unreal Engine from source, as it's needed for packaging a dedicated server project. ### Identity Center vs IAM

So we have an AWS account and we're logged in as the root user. As we've mentioned previously, the root user has full permission to access and change important settings in our AWS account, such as billing information. AWS best practice is to not use the root user for daily use, but instead to create a designated user which has restricted permissions even if that designated user has administrative permissions, which is very broad and has access to a great deal of AWS services. The typical process for this used to be to create an IAM user, IAM standing for Identity and Access Management, and there's an IAM console in AWS where identity and access can be managed. An IAM user is a digital identity that you create to provide specific permissions so they can access AWS services and resources. IAM users have their own credentials and can be assigned unique permissions to perform different tasks. A newer feature in AWS is the Identity Center, formerly known as AWS. Single Sign On, or SSL, is a service that simplifies managing access to multiple AWS accounts and applications. With Identity Center, you can centrally manage users and their access and allow them to sign on with a single set of credentials. This streamlines user management, enhances security, and can also easily integrate with existing third party identity providers and Identity Center. Users can access multiple AWS accounts with customized permissions for that access, and they don't have to log in to separate AWS accounts with separate credentials, as an IAM user would have to do. So the key differences between IAM users and Identity Center users are the following. Management scope. IAM users are managed individually within each AWS account, while Identity Center users can be managed centrally even for multiple AWS accounts and applications. While this may not pertain to us directly, as we are a single user with a single AWS account, it's still good practice to set up Identity Center and create an Identity Center user, giving us the ability to sign on with a single set of credentials, and in the future, we can even integrate multiple AWS accounts and manage their permissions and access easily. There's also Federation Identity Center users support federated identities. What does this mean? Well, it means that users can log in with credentials from external identity providers, which IAM users don't support natively. This also may not pertain to us either, but it's useful to know about identity. Users also have single sign on capabilities. They can access multiple AWS accounts and applications with a single login, while IAM users need separate credentials for each AWS account. AWS is used by many different companies, and as a company's operations grow large, they may involve teams of developers each having their own AWS accounts and each contributing to the project. Managing access and permissions from a single centralized place can make this a much easier project to manage. So if you're new to all this, you may be wondering which type of user to create an IAM user or an identity center user. Well, AWS best practice is to set up Identity Center and create an Identity center user. So we'll be following best practices and creating an identity center user for our daily use. While we can restrict permissions to this user, we'll be giving it administrative access, which will grant it access to most AWS services, making it easy for us to learn all the services throughout the course without pausing to grant the user access to services one by one. But Identity Center users don't automatically gain access to the underlying AWS accounts billing information, for example. So our root user account won't be used for daily use, as that's considered bad practice. AWS also recommends, but doesn't require, creating an identity center organization. This allows us to manage multiple AWS accounts centrally, and while you may not have multiple AWS accounts working on your project, you may in the future. So we'll set this up as recommended by AWS, and it's perfectly valid to have an organization with a single account. And all of this is covered under the free tier, so we might as well follow best practices and do it the way AWS recommends. So let's get started creating an Identity Center user for daily access in AWS.

Arn stands for Amazon Resource Name, and it's a unique identifier used to reference AWS resources. Every time we create a new resource in AWS, such as a permission set, that resource has an Arn to identify it. And it's really useful because many of the AWS services reference each other and use each other, and they can reference each other by their Arn. You can think of it as a complete address for any resource within AWS, and it ensures that AWS services and applications can correctly identify and interact with each other. The provision status of a permission set indicates whether the permission set has been successfully applied to the target AWS accounts. When a permission set is provisioned, it means that the necessary IAM roles and policies have been created and assigned in the specified accounts, so we have not assigned this administrator access permission set yet. ## GameLift Fleets

### Virtual Machines Basics

Welcome back. In this section we're going to learn how to deploy our dedicated servers in the cloud on a virtual machine. So the first question we must answer is why you may have a game that you wish to make, and have that game hosted on a dedicated server for your clients to connect to. You might have thought that you'd have to host this on your computer, or perhaps buy a machine that you can dedicate to hosting the game. Now, some games do this, and it's a valid choice to host on your own resources. There are some drawbacks, however. First, what happens when your player base increases? You may have spent a lot of money on a powerful beast machine that can run several dedicated server instances at a time, but what do you do when you need to now host a hundred games, or 1000 or 10,000? You would then need to buy more physical machines until you've scaled your operation into a server room, which does sound pretty cool, but there are several disadvantages to this. For one, your entire game is dependent on the reliability of your server room to remain in operation. If your server room goes out due to a power outage or a natural disaster, for instance, all of your players are kicked out of the game, which can be a huge hit to the player experience. You could plan for redundancy and set up a server room in a separate location, but this costs double the money that it takes to house a single server room, not only for the power hardware and maintenance, but to pay for the location as well. But there's another inefficiency we haven't yet considered. When you host games on your own hardware, you're rarely utilizing 100% of the machine's compute capacity. And if you are, you're dangerously close to experiencing performance hits because of resource exhaustion. When game activity decreases, you're still running 100% of your hardware and paying for it. You're also paying for someone to manage and maintain those servers, fixing things when they break, which involves game interruptions. When servers need to restart or get repaired. Things take longer when managing your own hardware, and this requires more humans to maintain the physical infrastructure. Aside from hardware redundancy, you might also want your game to be available to players in other geographical locations, including other countries across the globe. This becomes even more expensive to secure a location where you can run your servers in another country, and people to help manage it there too. All of this becomes easier when you utilize a service that can host your game or application on a virtual machine. This comes with several benefits, including lower costs, more availability, more redundancy without the effort to set up that infrastructure. This is beginning to sound like an ad, and at this point, I'd like to point out that I'm not being sponsored or paid or benefited in any way by Amazon or AWS. I'm simply laying out the benefits to using this pattern for game deployment. A company like Amazon has seemingly endless resources. They have a huge number of physical servers with staggering compute capabilities and storage. They have servers housed in locations all across the world, and you have the ability to utilize them from within the AWS console in any magnitude your project needs. So how does a virtual machine work and what benefits does it afford us? When you spin up your game server on a virtual machine in AWS, some poor IT guy doesn't go and rush down to the server room and boot up a machine for you. What really goes on is that servers are already up and available, each with a large amount of compute resources that can be accessed. The virtualization process is performed by a hypervisor, a technology that allows multiple operating systems to run on a physical machine by allocating hardware resources to each one. So a single physical machine with five terabytes of storage, for example, can be compartmentalized into multiple virtual machines, each sharing a portion of the overall storage. They share a portion of the CPU usage and memory as well. So you're effectively renting a portion of the machine's compute resources, specifying the hardware specs and operating system that your virtual machine requires to run your game. This gives several benefits. For one, you can rent specs that you need to run your game and no more. When you don't need the resources, you can shut them down, avoiding paying for those resources when you're done with them. If you house your own servers, you still have to pay for the maintenance and the power consumption of those servers. AWS manages the maintenance of its own hardware. You simply pay to use it while you need it. It's also always available, and you can specify the geographical locations that you want your software to run in. AWS has servers in different regions, and you can deploy your servers in different regions to provide players in or close to those regions access to the servers that are physically closer to them, resulting in a better play experience and lower ping times. Each AWS region has multiple availability Zones, which are separate locations within that region running on different subnets within your AWS, VPC, or Virtual Private Cloud. VPCs are isolated sections of the AWS cloud, and by default you have one for each region, essentially assigning you your own data center in the cloud where all of your AWS services run. You can take advantage of these availability zones for redundancy without needing to house your own physical hardware in different locations. All this makes it easy to make your game or application available to users without needing to set up your own physical infrastructure. And if you choose the appropriate services and resources, you can host a game or application for a much smaller cost than it would take you to set this all up on your own. In AWS, the way to run a virtual machine is to make use of the EC2 instance. EC2 is short for Elastic Cloud Compute. The elastic part means that you can scale up or down the usage to meet your needs, and an EC2 instance is a resource in AWS where you specify the compute specs for the virtual machine that you need to run your server. In Gamelift, EC2 instances are associated with gamelift fleets. A fleet is a collection of virtual computing resources. We've seen that we can create an anywhere fleet, which allowed us to specify our own machines as the compute resource, but we can also make gamelift managed fleets, where the compute resources are EC2 instances that we set up to run our game. Once we run a dedicated server build on an EC2 instance, we can manage it within the Gamelift console, access its details there or from the CLI, and we can create game sessions for that fleet, allowing us to access the IP address and port of that dedicated server so clients can connect to it and play on it. The free tier does include EC2 instances for Gamelift, specifically the C5 Large Compute Type, offering 125 hours of use under the free tier. So in the videos to come, we'll be configuring our game server to be able to run on an EC2 instance, upload our packaged server build to Gamelift, create a Gamelift managed fleet, and learn how to connect to it from clients. So let's get started.

## AWS Lambda

### Serverless

Welcome back. We're now going to learn about my absolute favorite AWS resource, the AWS Lambda. When you hear talk of AWS lambdas, you often hear the term serverless. So let's talk about what that means. First of all, don't let the misnomer fool you. All code has to run on someone's server somewhere, and lambdas are no different. What lambdas allow is for your code to be run on someone else's server for seconds or minutes at a time. We can design code that reacts to external events, whether those are set up to trigger automatically or executed manually. We can write code in an AWS Lambda that can access our AWS resources and manipulate them. We can create Gamelift game sessions and player sessions, access databases, verify our own custom requirements. When someone logs in as a user to our game or creates a new account for our game, etc., our Lambda code runs in its own isolated environment. An AWS lambdas have access to the AWS SDKs, and we can choose from a variety of programming languages to write our lambdas logic. Since our client builds of our Unreal Engine projects aren't packaged with the AWS server SDK, they have no access to AWS APIs. What they can do, however, is send a message to an endpoint on AWS to trigger a Lambda. We can even implement security measures so that no one can do this without the proper credentials. You can have a lambda that sits idle for weeks or months, never executing, and you never get billed for it until it becomes active. On the other hand, you can have a massive number of lambda requests to run code in your lambda all at the same time, and Lambda will scale up to execute all of those requests simultaneously. So this model scales for large scale operations automatically. Lambdas are an extremely powerful tool, and once you get the hang of how to write them, you'll see that the AWS Lambda is a very important component to your cloud architecture, allowing you to access and manipulate data in your cloud environment very easily. So we'll get started getting to know the Lambda console in AWS. We'll learn how to write our first Lambda, how to test it, and we'll learn about the format for data that we can pass into a lambda, as well as the data returned in a lambdas output response. We can choose from different programming languages for our lambdas, and while it's expected that students of this course already know C plus plus, we won't be writing our lambdas in C Plus plus as the syntax gets unwieldy and verbose. And there are simpler languages that make lambda coding much easier. I've opted to use Node.js for our lambdas, which is a very easy and natural language for any C plus plus developer to learn. NodeJS is a JavaScript runtime designed to be run on servers rather than within a web browser, which is what JavaScript is known for. The syntax is similar and the code is more concise for programming our serverless functions. I'm not assuming that you already know Node.js. In fact, I'm assuming that you don't. So we'll introduce the basics of Node.js. And aside from a few syntactical differences from C plus plus, you'll find that you'll pick it up quickly and easily. Think of it sort of like C plus plus without the pointers and references and other low level features that make C plus plus harder than most other languages. So let's get started learning AWS Lambda. I'll see you in the next video.

----------------------------------------

### Anatomy of a Lambda Function

Welcome back. So let's talk about the anatomy of an AWS Lambda. When we author a Lambda from scratch, we get this code as a starting point. The most important thing to understand is that all lambdas must have a handler function. A handler in AWS is the main entry point for the Lambda function. When the lambda is executed, it starts with the handler. This line is the function declaration. So let's break down this function piece by piece. Handler is the function name const means that we're defining a constant reference to this function. The reference called handler can't be assigned to anything else. The function itself can still execute and performs its operations, but you can't change the fact that handler is the name pointing to this specific function. Export is like giving a gift that can be opened elsewhere. When you use export before a function or a variable. You're making it accessible to other files or modules. You're saying that this function or variable can be imported into other parts of an application. Lambda relies on this fact so that it can run the handler function in response to AWS events. Async means that this function is declared as asynchronous. This means that certain operations can occur without blocking the execution of the entire program. We can execute some operation which may take some time to finish, and our code execution doesn't have to stop and wait for it unless we want it to. Retrieving information from a database, for example, may take a small bit of time to finish, and therefore is something we can do asynchronously, and we can even place code in our lambda to wait for those async actions to finish before we continue. Event is the input that is passed into this function when the lambda executes. It contains information from the invoker of the function, and this can change depending on the lambda and what triggers it. It's passed in as a JSON formatted string, and the runtime converts it into an object called event. We'll soon see the relationship between JSON formatted data and JavaScript objects. Const response declares a constant variable called response which holds a JavaScript object. The opening and closing braces just after the equals sign on response denote the object literal. JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means that the variable can hold values of different types at runtime, and we also say that it's weakly typed, meaning that variables don't need to be bound to a specific data type. So we have more flexibility when it comes to the types for our variables. Now let's look inside the braces that come just after the equals sign on response. Notice we have some key value pairs consisting of a name a colon followed by a value. Status code is a property of the response object. Properties are key value pairs, where statuscode is the key and 200 is the value which has the type number. So you might be used to specific types of numbers like integers and floating point values. In JavaScript, they're all under the category of number. Properties are separated by commas. As you can see. After statuscode comes the next property called body. Body is a property with the key of body and it's assigned the value here returned from the Stringify function. Json.stringify will convert an object into a string, and it's not technically needed here, as hello from Lambda is already a string literal. String literals are denoted by single quotes or double quotes, but json.stringify is a nice function as it can accept JavaScript objects as input, and Stringify will convert that object to a JSON formatted string, so we'll see plenty of use of it, even if it's not strictly necessary. In this use case, the return statement specifies that the response object should be returned to the invoker of this lambda. This is how we can retrieve data from a lambda once we've called it from elsewhere. In lambdas, we often package the response like this in an object with a status code and a body. As the status code can indicate the success or failure of the lambda, we use codes, and 200 is the status code that we use for a successful request. There are other codes that denote failure, and we can identify the type of error based on the value of the status code. If you've ever seen the error code 404 and a web browser, you're familiar with error codes, as 404 indicates that the resource was not found. And finally, we have a comment denoted by the double slash. Like in C plus plus comments are ignored, so we can treat the handler as the entry point for our lambda, and any code that we place in its body will be executed when the lambda function runs. Let's get some practice testing our lambda. We'll do so in the next video. I'll see you soon.

### Try Catch

Welcome back. In this video we're going to talk about try catch blocks, which is something you might not be used to in Unreal Engine as we don't use try catch in unreal. In unreal, we opt for the use of assertions which allow us to halt the execution of our program when some condition is not met. Games tend to be more performant that way as performance is critical. Try catch blocks in lambdas are pretty common because they allow us to try something, such as executing a command and handling any errors that might arise. And we can do anything we like. In the case of an error such as retry sending that command, and so on. Now to create a try catch block, it's pretty easy. We simply use try followed by a block of code. And immediately after that block we catch. Now catch has an input for the error. If any error is thrown. The catch block will catch the error stored in this error object, and this allows us to have any sort of logic we like in response to the error. So we can place these lines where we're sending the command in the try block. In fact, we can even return early by including the return response line of code. So we can cut these and place them right here in the try. And in the case of an error, we can catch that error. So what do we do in the case of an error. Well we can return the error. We can also return a JavaScript object where we decide on the status code and the body. For instance, we can say that status code is 500, which is basically a general distress signal that's sent out when the server encounters an unexpected condition that prevents it from fulfilling the request. We can specify a body as well, and that body could be descriptive of the error. In fact, we could use Json.stringify and stringify the error object. Now the return statement does need a semicolon. So now we've wrapped this in a try catch block. And if we don't encounter any errors from this command we're attempting, then we should just return the response. Now the response does have its own status and its own body of information, as does the error itself. The error itself will have its own error code, which may be different than the 500 we're specifying here, but we can specify 500 for the response of our lambda function, whereas the error itself may have a different error code. Now we can deploy these changes, and we can run this test by testing our list fleets test event. And in this case our response contains the simple response object, so it has its own status code 200. If you don't want all of this information, you can specify what you return. ## API Gateway

### API Gateway - Our Plan

Welcome back. So we know how to create lambdas. And we've seen that they can take in input data in JSON format. And that lambdas also return output also in JSON format. And we tested our lambdas in the Lambda console which was easy enough. But ultimately we'd like to trigger these lambdas from within our Unreal Engines Cplusplus code. So how can this be done? The missing piece to this puzzle is the HTTP request. HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It's the foundation of any data exchange on the web, and is a protocol used for transferring hypertext requests and information between servers and browsers. Hypertext refers to text displayed on a computer display or other device, with references or hyperlinks to other text that the reader can access. Think of an HTTP request as a letter that you send to the server asking for information or to perform an action. An HTTP request consists of several key parts. The method which indicates what type of action you're requesting, method types are get, put, post, delete, and so on. The URL, which is an address of the resource that you want to access. Headers which contain metadata about the request such as the content type, authorization, etc., and an optional body which contains data that you're sending with the request. Usually used with the put or post methods. Each time you open a web page, there's an HTTP request working behind the scenes. Each of the method types are used for different actions. Get is used to retrieve data from the server. An example would be getting a user's profile information. Get operations are safe and idempotent, meaning that the action can be repeated without changing anything. Post is used to create a new resource on the server. An example would be submitting a registration form to create a new user account. This action is not idempotent, meaning that repeating the same request can result in creating multiple resources. Put is used to update an existing resource or create one if it doesn't exist. An example would be updating user details or preferences. This action is idempotent, as repeating the same request produces the same result, and delete is used to remove a resource from the server. An example would be deleting a user's account. This action is idempotent, since repeating the request ultimately results in the same outcome. We can send HTTP requests from within our Unreal Engine cplusplus code. When we do, we must specify the above characteristics such as the method, URL, headers, and body, and our request will be sent to the URL specified. While lambdas have the ability to have their own HTTP URLs, meaning that we can send an HTTP request directly to a lambda, there's a better practice than this. AWS has a service called API gateway. We can create our own APIs application programming interfaces. Selecting from among several choices, we can create Rest APIs. Rest stands for Representational State Transfer. These are used for creating, reading, updating, and deleting resources using HTTP methods. APIs with these features, which are typically stateless, are known as RESTful. We can create HTTP APIs, which are also RESTful, but come with less features than Rest APIs in API gateway. Things that Rest APIs have, such as API keys per client, throttling, request validation, private API endpoints are all features present in Rest APIs, but not present in HTTP APIs, and thus HTTP APIs are cheaper. We can also create WebSocket APIs which allow for full duplex communication. In other words, they open a two way interaction system for the client and server to communicate back and forth. The AWS server SDK that we set up on our dedicated server build makes use of WebSockets to connect to Gamelift under the hood, as we needed to get that WebSocket URL endpoint. For our purposes, a rest API is perfect. We can create our own resources, each with one or more methods that have their own endpoint URLs. Calling these methods can trigger the execution of our lambdas. Forwarding the HTTP request data to them. Doing it this way gives us several benefits. With API gateway we have centralized management. API gateway provides a single entry point for all your APIs, making it easier to manage, monitor and update them. Security API gateway offers built in security features like throttling, authentication, and authorization, ensuring that only valid requests reach your Lambda functions. Scalability. API gateway can handle a large number of requests and automatically scale to meet demand, without you having to manage the infrastructure. Versioning. You can manage different versions of your APIs, allowing you to roll out new features and updates without disrupting existing users. Monitoring and logging. API gateway provides detailed monitoring and logging capabilities, helping you track usage, performance and errors and caching. API gateway is capable of caching responses, reducing the load on your Lambda functions and improving the response times of your users. These features make API gateway a solid choice for handling applications and managing the execution of our lambdas, and its console makes it extremely easy and quick to set up. So we need a game plan for tying together our Unreal Engine game project with our cloud services. An API gateway is the key to making this happen. In a game or application. We typically have some UI presented to the user in the form of text boxes or buttons. In Unreal Engine, these exist in the form of widgets. So when we click a button widget, some code is executed in response, and we need that code to result in sending an HTTP request to somewhere to an endpoint. In other words, that endpoint will be one that we set up in our API gateway. Each endpoint that we set up will be associated with one or more HTTP methods, get, Post, etc. and these methods will be linked up with lambda functions that will receive the HTTP request data in their event input objects. We'll send the request to the endpoint, which will trigger the lambda, and our Lambda will harvest and use the data in the event access our resources through AWS SDK calls and return a response back in Unreal Engine, we'll receive the response and perform the appropriate action, such as taking that response data, parsing it, and using it to update the game, such as updating the text in our widgets. So how do we architect all this? First, we create our widgets. These will have the interactable parts that the user will interact with, such as buttons and text boxes. But a widgets job should be limited. Widgets are meant to show user facing data and take in input. Sending an HTTP request is too much responsibility for a simple widget class, so we'll create a special class to handle HTTP request code. This can be as lightweight as a simple UI object that can respond to the widget inputs. We press a button and tell this Uobject to send the request. Receive and parse the response and send it back to the widgets to display the information. We'll start with a simple example. By creating a widget with a button and our uobject, we'll call it the HTTP request manager, as well as a data asset that can store our API gateway endpoints that we need for our HTTP requests. Since ultimately we'd like to consider security for all this. We'll later make use of API gateways, authentication, and authorization features by requiring that certain HTTP requests contain an authentication token in their headers, but we'll need a way to get that auth token for specific users, and that will come later. For now, we simply need to learn how to create our gateway so that we can execute our lambdas from within our Unreal Engine code. What's cool about all this is that you can send HTTP requests from any Unreal Engine project, whether multiplayer or not, even from testing within a Pi session and even while running in debug mode. This means that we can place breakpoints in our code at various stages of this process to examine the data we're working with. So our plan involves the following steps. First, we'll create an API gateway with an endpoint tied to an HTTP request method linking our Lambda function to it. We'll create a basic widget class with a button to trigger the HTTP request, and some widgets to show the response. We'll make a data asset class that can store the URL endpoints that are HTTP requests will need, and we'll make an HTTP request manager with the code to perform the actual request, receive the response, and parse it and pass it back to the widget. And then we'll test our system, making sure that we can successfully perform these actions. Since this is all architecture that you may wish to reuse in multiple projects, it helps to keep this code isolated from the main project and independent of it. That way it can be reused in any number of projects and situations. For this reason, it's a good practice to create a separate module independent of our main Game Projects module. This separate module will contain all of this cloud functionality, and this keeps a strict separation of concerns. And our code is more flexible, modular, scalable, and more easily testable. Once we have this process down, we can expand it by creating more lambdas, associate those with API gateway endpoints, and expand our game's capabilities to be able to perform more actions, such as searching for game sessions, creating a game session if none exists yet, creating a player session for the game session that was found, and actually joining the game. We'll then learn how we can accept the player session on the server. So Gamelift updates the status of our player sessions and will terminate our player sessions when players leave the server. This makes our game's user experience much better, as we will no longer need to use the CLI to create our game sessions from the command line and do things like find the server's IP address and port and so on. So let's get started. I'll see you in the next video.

### Creating a Module

Welcome back. So we need a module. And there are multiple ways to make a module in Unreal Engine. You can even make one from within the Unreal Engine editor. Now to do so within Visual Studio requires that you have the Visual Studio Unreal integration tools, which you may or may not have in your project. But it's actually quite simple. And we're going to use the most basic way to make a module that will work for everybody, whether you're using Visual Studio or Writer, and this will be the most bare bones way to do it. So we go into our source folder and we make a new folder here. And this folder name is going to be the name of our module. And I'd like our module to be called Dedicated Servers because it's going to contain all of that specific code for dedicated servers, namely the code that we use to access the cloud. You'll see them with the name of your root folder for the module, with the word module appended to it. It doesn't really matter, but we'll create those header and cpp files. That's one way to do it, but another way to do it is to make use of the JSON object converter, which is capable of converting a JSON object into a struct, which is a very nice feature. So to use the JSON object converter, we have to create a struct, and that struct has to have the same fields as the JSON object, including matching names. For instance, if we create a struct to take in metadata that struct corresponding to the metadata JSON object has to have values corresponding to these properties in the JSON object, and we know that the status code is implemented as a number as its type, and we know that the request ID is implemented as a string. The attempts is implemented as a number, and the total retry delay is implemented as a number. So we can create a struct that has these four properties with the same names. And the JSON object converter can convert the JSON object into a struct whose member variables have these values. So that means we need to create a struct. I'm going to go ahead and stop the process, and we can create a struct to store our metadata. And we're going to have different types for the different responses from our HTTP requests. So we're going to create a use struct I'm going to define a struct. And this struct is going to be for storing metadata. Now I would call it f metadata. But metadata is a name used by the engine that's going to create a conflict. Even though the engine's metadata is a U metadata, it'll still cause a conflict. And we're going to define our struct. We need a generated body. Don't let writer trick you into using generated you struct body. These use generated body just like you classes do. Now, even though the status code is a number in the JSON object, which is stored as a double, we can still make it an int32 in our struct. It'll be implicitly converted into an int, and as long as you know that this particular number is a whole number, such as a status code, you can use an int32. So we're going to call this HTTP status code. And I'm going to go ahead and initialize it using braced initialization. Equals. Double equals is known as loose equality, which compares two values for equality after converting both values to a common type if necessary. This can involve a type conversion. For instance, if we said five double equals a string called five, well this would be true. So it's quite lax. It's a loose equality. What we want is strict equality. The triple equals. This is going to fail if you check something like five triple equals the string five. This would fail. This would be false. And that's what we like when checking equality. We want the triple equals for strict equality. And we're going to check to see if this status is equal to all caps active. So we're looping over the fleet attributes. ## AWS Cognito

### AWS Cognito

Welcome back. When you buy a video game and start it up for the first time, you're not typically thrown straight into the gameplay right away. There's usually a sign up process that allows you to create an account for the game. You typically create an account linked to your email address, and create a password so that you can log into the game. So why do games have their players create an account for the game? Having an account serves several purposes for a game or application in general. User accounts allow games to save your progress, achievements, and in-game items. This way you can pick up where you left off even if you switch devices. Accounts enable personalized settings and recommendations based on your gaming preferences and behavior. Many games include social features like friend lists, leaderboards, and multiplayer modes. User accounts facilitate these social interactions. Accounts help ensure that only authorized users can access certain features of content, and they help prevent cheating or misuse. Developers can track in-game purchases and manage subscriptions through user accounts. This also allows them to offer personalized promotions or discounts. And user accounts provide valuable data about player behavior, which developers can use to improve the game and tailor future updates. Having user accounts is a feature that any game can have, whether it's multiplayer or not. In modern times, even single player games often have users create accounts to take advantage of the above features, and you can implement user accounts even if your game never connects to a dedicated server at all. We've seen that we can trigger serverless functions in the cloud to access AWS resources. Even when the client build running the game hasn't even connected to a game server in AWS. The way to create user accounts for your game is through the use of the AWS service, known as Cognito. Amazon Cognito is a comprehensive identity management platform offered by AWS. It provides tools for user authentication, authorization, and user management. Key features include. User pools manage user directories with features like signup, sign in, and password management. It can even be integrated with social identity providers like Google, Facebook, and Apple. Identity pools are a feature that allow you to grant temporary limited privilege. AWS credentials to access other AWS services. This allows you to authenticate users through various identity providers and manage access to your resources. Federated Identity means a user's identity can be verified across multiple systems or organizations using a single set of credentials. Incognito has advanced security features built in. For our purposes, we'll be using Cognito to create user pools for our game. A Cognito user pool is a directory where you can manage and authenticate users for your games and applications. It allows users to sign up and sign in to gain access to the game or app. When a new player signs up, a user is added to the user pool for that player. Users can have unique credentials and provide information managed within the user pool, and the process of signing in can grant them access to the game or app and permission to perform specific actions. We'll be creating a sign in page with the capability to create new user accounts and verify them with an email verification code. They can then sign in to those accounts and play the game as that specific user. We'll be saving persistent data to databases in the AWS cloud and associating that data with the user that that information is stored for. This allows for all sorts of things, like saving a player's progress, creating leaderboards and saving in-game items, and so on. To create our own user pool, first we'll get to know the Cognito console in AWS. We'll create a new user pool, allowing us to store a directory of users for our game. We'll then create a sign in menu system with widgets that can switch between sign up, sign in, and verification screens. We'll then create AWS lambdas that can perform Cognito API actions, such as creating new users and logging in. We'll associate those lambdas with a Rest API that will create an API gateway. Creating endpoints so that our in-game code can send HTTP requests for these API calls, and then we'll tie it all together by implementing the functionality for our sign in menu system, so users can create new accounts and sign in from within the game. Once a user is logged in, we can grant them authorization to perform actions such as finding or creating game sessions, creating player sessions, and accessing the IP address and port of a dedicated server game to join. We'll restrict our APIs so that only HTTP requests that contain the proper credentials with specific permissions can trigger our API endpoints. And we'll now have the specific users that we can identify and associate with persistent data that we can save in the cloud. Then when we learn how to create cloud databases, we'll be able to store data for specific users in our user pools. So let's get started learning the Cognito console in AWS. I'll see you in the next video.

### Separation of Concerns

Welcome back. We're going to talk a little bit about separation of concerns, a very important topic in programming. As our projects are going to get bigger and bigger. That's what projects do. And it's important to separate concerns in order to keep things modular and scalable. Let's talk about our HTTP request managers for a minute. We have a class called HTTP Request Manager. This is the base class that we've inherited from when we created our Portal Manager class. Now the HTTP request manager has some properties such as a data asset for API URLs, and each of our HTTP request manager child classes is meant to do the heavy lifting, so our widgets don't have to send HTTP requests. Now, so far we've added some functionality to our Portal manager. It has the ability to join game sessions. It sends HTTP requests to find an active game session or create one if it doesn't exist, and it also has the capability to try creating a player session. It creates a player session for a given game session so that we have the ability to join that game session, but now we're adding more functionality to it. Regarding signing in and signing up for users in our Cognito user pool, we've already created functions for signup, confirm, sign up, and sign in. We haven't implemented these just yet in our Portal Manager, but these are related to Cognito. So our Portal Manager is starting to have more responsibilities than it should now. This is natural. When programming, we start adding features and capabilities, and classes can tend to gain extra responsibilities, but it's important to recognize when that happens so that we can manage it. Now these are really two categories of functionality, and they're actually tied to different APIs in our Amazon API gateway. It's good practice to separate these actions into different APIs. Because they can be managed separately, their permissions can be managed separately as well. Now, this set of functionality is tied to our Game Sessions API, and we even have a data asset that contains the API URLs for the endpoints in our Game Sessions API. Whereas this set of functionality is related to our Cognito API, which we call the portal API, and we created a separate data asset for those endpoints. Now our HTTP request manager only has one variable for a data asset that stores our API data. Right? And while we could add multiple variables for multiple data assets in our HTTP request managers, I'd rather not do that because each HTTP request manager should be responsible for managing the API calls for a single API. This allows us to keep a separation of concerns. So our portal manager now has too many responsibilities. What we can do instead is we can create multiple child classes of our HTTP request manager. We can create a new type of manager specifically to manage game session related actions. And this can be a separate class from our portal manager which manages our Cognito related actions. Things like signing in and signing up. And each of these can have their own data assets. We can associate a game sessions manager with the Game Sessions API and give it that Game Sessions API data data asset. That way we have a separate class for each type of manager, and any given widget can use one or more of these. This allows us to make use of composition rather than inheritance, and composition is a very powerful tool when programming. Object oriented programming is great and it has its own strengths, but a component based architecture can be more scalable and is often preferred as objects scale up for certain situations. So with composition, an object can be composed of other objects with a has a relationship rather than is a. In other words, we don't have to inherit from a class to gain functionality from it. We can simply have a subclass treating these more like components, not components in an Unreal Engine actor component, since as these are just you objects, but we can add one of these objects to any class to give it the capability of managing HTTP requests. So for that reason, we're going to separate our concerns and allow our portal manager to handle signing in signing up those portal related API calls, and we'll create a new manager for game sessions. And that can handle things like finding and creating game sessions, creating player sessions, and so on. So we'll perform this separation of concerns in the next video. And this is going to make our code much more easily manageable, easier to test and debug. And overall it'll be a better solution and will be adhering to better coding practices. I'll see you soon.

----------------------------------------

### Dependency Injection

Welcome back. So we have a local player subsystem. If we go to that class we'll see that it has a pointer to the portal manager. And this allows it to use those nice features on the portal manager, namely its HTTP request capabilities. But there's just one thing. Our portal manager has a dependency on our local player subsystem. And if these two classes have dependencies on each other, they're tightly coupled, which makes for a less flexible design. So in general, we try to keep our dependencies at least one way, resulting in loose coupling and more flexible design. So the question now arises how can we maintain a flexible design while still retaining this relationship between the two classes? Well, one common method is dependency injection. Now we are injecting a dependency on the portal manager into our local player subsystem here, but it would be more flexible if local player subsystem did not depend directly on the portal manager, but still was able to access functionality on it. Now there are different ways to eliminate this circular dependency, but the way that I would prefer in this case is to make use of an interface. Interfaces are nice because if our local player subsystem depends on an interface rather than the portal manager class itself, then we could add that functionality that we need to. Literally any class and the local player subsystem will just depend on the interface itself. And if it holds a pointer to that interface, then it can simply access that functionality without accessing the class, the portal manager. So we're going to create an interface that our portal manager can implement. And then any class can access that functionality through the interface. So I'm going to open up my portal folder here where we have the portal manager. And I'd like to make a new folder here called interfaces. And we'll create a new unreal interface here. So I'm going to have the interfaces folder in portal in the public section, as well as in the portal folder in the private section. So in the private section I'm going to go ahead and add a new directory called interfaces. Now we can create a new interface in this interfaces folder. So I'm going to right click add a new unreal class and choose interface. And this will be for managing functionality on the portal. So I'm going to call it Portal Management. So let's create this interface. And the only thing that our local player subsystem needs from the portal is the functionality of refreshing the tokens. So our portal manager has a refresh tokens function. We can see in DS local player subsystem dot cpp that it's just accessing the portal manager and calling this refresh tokens function, which requires an f string by const reference. So our new portal management interface can simply have a refresh tokens function. We can declare this as virtual. It'll be void and it'll be called refresh tokens. And it'll take a const f string reference called refresh token. And we can make this pure virtual. So not only do we not have to define it here in the interface, but any class that implements this interface must implement refresh tokens. And that's going to be our portal manager. So let's open Portal Manager and add this dependency on the IE portal management class. So we're going to inherit from AI portal management. And that means we're going to have to include the portal management header file here in interfaces, and we now have to implement refresh tokens. Now we already have refresh tokens but it's being defined here. It's not a virtual override but we can make it one. We can add virtual and override. Technically just the override is what's necessary. But we tend to mark virtual on those functions just to make it clear. And I typically like to put these under a comment that shows the interface that we're implementing here. So I'm going to say I portal management and we'll just keep it there. Now that's the only change we need for the portal manager. It now implements this interface. And it already has the definition for refresh tokens. So now we can strip away that dependency on the portal manager class here in our local player subsystem. But instead we can use the I portal management interface. So instead of having a t object pointer to you portal manager, we can now have a member variable of this AI Portal Management interface class. And if we're going to have a member variable that's a pointer to an interface. The recommended practice is to use the T script interface wrapper. So we'll have a T script interface to AI portal management. And we'll call this portal management interface. And t script interface gives us type safety and some other perks such as exposure to blueprints if you need that functionality and so on. So T script interface is the recommended way to have a member variable to an unreal interface. So when we inject the dependency on the portal management interface we'll do it in initialize tokens here. So I'm going to change initialize tokens to. Now take in a t script interface to AI portal management. And we'll just call it portal management. So we'll go ahead and change the function declaration as well as the function definition. So we'll now no longer depend on you. Portal manager will depend on portal management instead and will set portal management interface equal to the portal management input parameter here. And now all we need to do here. Instead of calling refresh tokens directly on the portal manager, we'll first check to make sure that our portal management interface has a valid object. So as we're checking is valid on the world we'll also place another is valid check. And this time we're going to take our portal management interface. And this wrapper t script interface has the function Getobject. And that allows us to get the actual object that implements the interface. And we can make sure that that is a valid object. And as long as that object implements the interface properly and t script interface helps to enforce that. We can simply call refresh tokens on the portal management interface instead. And now that we depend on the interface and not the You Portal Manager object, we can replace the Include to Portal Manager with UI portal slash interfaces, slash portal management, and we can even forward declare this I Portal Management interface class here instead of US Portal Manager. And now our local player subsystem is independent of the Portal Manager and depends on the interface class instead. So I'm done with the portal management interface. I can close those and my portal manager has now implemented I Portal Management and implemented the Refresh tokens pure virtual function, providing its own implementation of it. And so now we have a cleaner system that's now loosely coupled. And we no longer have that circular Dependency of the local player subsystem and the portal manager, so things are a bit cleaner. Now keep in mind that the portal manager is not going to persist like our local player subsystem does. Our local player subsystem will remain even when we travel to the server and travel between levels, whereas the portal manager is just a new object. So it's important to understand that this is valid. Check to the get object call on the TypeScript interface will not return a valid object. If that portal manager has gone out of scope, and the portal manager would have still been destroyed, even if the local player subsystem had kept a uproperty pointer to it. As the portal manager is not a persistent class like the local player subsystem is. So that's just important to keep in mind that as soon as we leave the level which contains the sign in overlay and associated classes, then we're no longer going to be refreshing our tokens because the portal manager won't be alive anymore. So refreshing the tokens is really something that we just have when we're still in the sign in menu, or the portal system in general. As soon as we start going into actual matches, we're no longer refreshing those tokens. So a common thing that most games do is when you leave the game cycle and go back to the main menu, you would typically either sign in again or begin refreshing those tokens again, and so on, which is exactly what we're doing. If we go back to the sign in menu, then the process starts over again and we begin refreshing those tokens as soon as we sign in and get those initial tokens and call initialize tokens here. And of course, these systems can be designed in any number of ways, but that's just something to keep in mind. So now we have a nice loose coupled system where our local player subsystem no longer depends on the portal manager class. Great job. I'll see you soon.

### Custom Scopes (optional)

Welcome back. So now that we're signing in and getting access tokens, it's time to start requiring those access tokens for some of our API calls. Now we can require an access token. And we can also require access tokens that have specific permissions. We implement that by creating custom scopes for the access token. Now, requiring an access token is something we can do under the free tier of AWS, but requiring an access token with a custom scope is not. That requires advanced security features which are not in the free tier. So while they're not expensive by any means, this video is optional because we're using something outside the free tier. So fair warning if you only want to use the free tier and you don't want to get any charges. You can opt out of using custom scopes. You can still require an access token, so you'll learn how to do that in this video. But you cannot use custom scopes unless you're okay with going outside the free tier and enabling those advanced security features. And if you don't want to do any of this, you can skip this video and the next video for pre token Lambda trigger custom scopes can be set up for our Cognito user pool. Let's go on over to the Cognito console and go to our user pool. In order to have a custom scope, we must set up a resource server in our user pool. Under App Integration, I'm going to click on App Integration and scroll down to Resource Servers. This is where you can define custom scopes and describe what they should be used for. Now for the hosted UI, which we're not really using anymore, that can grant custom scopes if you're using it, but for your own custom UI, you must add the custom scope to your access token and we'll get to how to do that. ### Pre Token Lambda Trigger (optional)

Welcome back. So we created a resource server where we defined one custom scope. And in our API gateway we created a Cognito authorizer called DS Game Sessions Authorizer where we're requiring an authorization header which has a custom scope inside of it specifically for our find or Create game sessions post method. ## Lobbies and Timers

### Lobbies, Timers, and Player Sessions

Welcome back. Now we've implemented a game dashboard. So as soon as we sign in and we get those access tokens, we have some menus. And the game menu contains a play button. And so far that play button just launches us into the first game session that we can find or creates one if it doesn't exist and creates a player session for us. And through that player session, we get the IP address and port and we travel to the server. Now this is great and if that's all that you care about, then fine. But often serious games have lobbies in which we store a collection of players as they're joining the game, and then as soon as enough players join, some sort of match or session is initiated. So our play button should actually take us to the server, but our server should be running some sort of lobby level waiting for players so that it can initiate some sort of match or session. Now, inevitably, when it comes to lobbies and waiting for players, we have to talk about the concept of timers. Let's just say that we design a lobby. Now the lobby could be anything. It could literally be a level where joining players possess pawns and run around. Or it could simply be strictly UI with an empty level showing a HUD to all players who join it. Now, this lobby may or may not be running a game session in a gamelift sense the very first time a player joins it. A game session can be made and can be waiting for players, and then as soon as a player joins the lobby, the lobby can decide whether or not to accept that player session, and that player session in Gamelift can be updated to the accepted status. So our lobby can be sitting here waiting. And as players join the lobby, their names can show up and we can display to all players waiting in the lobby how many players there are, who those players are. And at a certain point, as soon as some minimum number of players has joined, the lobby can start some kind of countdown so the players know how much time there is until the match actually starts. For this reason, our lobby will be in one of a number of different states. If there are no players yet, the lobby can simply be waiting for players to join. And as soon as enough players join, we can start that countdown to the game match, at which point our game mode can initiate a seamless travel and switch over to the match level and take all the connected players with it. Seamless travel is great for this, because the player controllers will persist in this seamless travel process, and any data stored on those player controllers will still be there once we get to the other level. Now, this countdown will have a timer running and when that timer finally finishes, we can start the seamless travel process, at which point our lobby level will be in the seamless traveling state for a brief period of time until that traveling process is complete. So until enough players join, the lobby will be waiting for players. When enough players join, the lobby will transition to the countdown, and we can even program it so that if some players leave during this countdown and the lobby goes down to zero or below some minimum number of players, the lobby can transition back to the state where it's waiting for players. And then as more players join, it can go back to the countdown. And when the countdown is up, the lobby can begin the seamless travel process. So timers play a role in lobby levels, but they also play a role in the actual match or game session that players travel to. For instance, you might have a game HUD in the actual game when players are playing and in the game there might be multiple timers running. There could be a pre-match timer where players can't move around yet they can just see that they're in the level. After that timer has elapsed, we may begin a match timer and as the players are playing the match, they can see how much time is left until the end of the match. And when the match is over, there's typically a post-match timer. Some period of time where statistics related to the match are relayed in a nice results widget, and players have to wait for a few seconds until the match either restarts or players are taken back to the lobby, and so on. So a match itself will have several possible states. It can be in the waiting for players state before any players join it. It can be in this state where no timers are running, and as soon as a minimum number of players or perhaps all the players join, the game mode can then transition into the pre-match state, starting a pre-match timer so everyone knows that in a few seconds the match will begin. When the match begins, the game can transition to the match state, where it can get rid of the pre-match timer and start the match timer, and after the match, the post-match state can begin showing the post-match timer, and when the post-match timer is finished, we can then initiate seamless traveling again, taking all those players back to the lobby, for example. So each of these states transitions into the next state during a match, and we can do things in response to transitioning to any of these states. For instance, when the match is over and we begin the post-match timer, transitioning to the post-match state is when we can display the match stats show the player how many eliminations and defeats they got, or special types of achievements. And this is a good point in time to save those stats to a database in the cloud so we can keep a record of the player's career, so we need timers to specify a point in time at which these actions occur. And when we talk about timers, especially ones that are authoritative running on the server, we have to talk about the difference between client and server time. Let's say we have a timer running on the server and it has a specific amount of seconds left. Let's just say it's counting down. And every so often our server wants to alert the client how much time there is left. So if there are five seconds left in the timer, the server can then send that data down to clients and tell them that they should show five seconds on their timers. So the server has its own version of the countdown. At any given point in time, that countdown timer has a value, and it's sending that data down to the client at specified intervals. But that data has to travel across the internet from the server to the client, sometimes across great distances and even with decent ping times, this trip will take some finite amount of time greater than zero. Now let's take a typical scenario where it takes about 22 milliseconds to reach the client. So the server says we have five seconds left. It sends that data to the client, and 22 milliseconds later, the client receives that value and updates its widgets to show five seconds left. This amount of time that the data took to get from the server to the client, we call single trip time, because it's the amount of time that the data took to make a single trip from server to client. Now, when the client sends data up to a server via an RPC, for instance, that data also takes time to get to the server. It has its own single trip time, and single trip time isn't Necessarily symmetrical, meaning that if data from the server took 22 milliseconds to. Reach the client, that doesn't necessarily mean that it's going to take. Exactly 22 milliseconds for the client to send data back to the server. In fact, these times are constantly varying. It just depends on the circumstances. Now, if we knew that it took 22 milliseconds for the server to send data to. The client, we could adjust the client's timer to account for that amount of time, but it's not very easy to know the single trip time. Exactly. One way to estimate the single trip time is to keep track of how long it takes to make a round trip. We call this the round trip time, and it's the time that it takes for data to go from server to client and back again. In other words, we add the two single trip times together. So if it takes 22 milliseconds for data to reach the client, and 18 milliseconds for data to reach the server from the client. We can add those two together for a total of 40 milliseconds round trip time, and we can estimate that single trip time by cutting this value in half. So we can say that on average, our single trip time between client and server is approximately 20 milliseconds. Now, this is incorrect. Of course, it takes 22 milliseconds in this hypothetical example, for data to reach the client from the server and 18 milliseconds to go back, but this gives us a pretty close approximation. It's only two milliseconds off in this hypothetical case, of course, and for most game purposes this approximation is enough. Two milliseconds is negligible, and when it comes to updating the client's timer to reflect what the server shows, it's more than accurate enough. So how do we account for the single trip time? Well, if the server says there's five seconds left in the timer and sends that off to the client. If we've made this single trip time estimation and we know that the single trip time is 20 milliseconds, then when the client receives that time of five seconds remaining, it can adjust by 20 milliseconds to account for the time that it took for that data to even reach the client. So if the server says there's five seconds left, and we know that there's about 20 milliseconds single trip time, then the client knows that it doesn't quite have five whole seconds left. It has a little bit less, about 20 milliseconds less. So on the server, the game mode or some server class can have a countdown timer running. Let's say it starts off at five seconds, and every so often at certain intervals, perhaps every second, it sends the data down to the client, telling the client how much time is left. Now, in the previous slide, our hypothetical example determined that the single trip time was 20 milliseconds, or 0.02 of a second. We can call it two centiseconds or two hundredths of a second. So when the client receives that data five seconds, it can adjust and its own locally running timer, if it has one can know that it doesn't have five seconds. It has four seconds and 98 centiseconds then server side, the server continues updating its timer and let's say one second later the server has four seconds left on its timer. It can send that data down to the client, and the client can receive four seconds, but it knows to adjust for 0.02 seconds or two centiseconds. So the client knows it doesn't actually have four seconds left. It's actually three seconds and 98 Centiseconds then server side, the server updates its timer again. Now it's down to three seconds. It sends that data down and the client receives the data. Adjusting for the single trip time again. So once we calculate this single trip time, we can adjust for that discrepancy between server and client. Now we can calculate the single trip time just once and continue to use that correction. And then each time the server updates that point in time at which the client receives that update, that's when the client can make the adjustment. Now the server could just tell the client at the start of the timer that we're starting the timer. Now go ahead and update your own timer locally and then never send another update again. But because of the inaccuracy between client and server and the fact that our single trip time is just an approximation, the timer is running on server and client are inevitably going to drift apart. It always happens. So a good way to compromise for this is for the server to update the timer and periodically tell the client what the current time is, and if the client is accounting for the single trip time, it's going to maintain its timer alongside the server with a very high degree of accuracy. In our hypothetical case, it'll only be two centiseconds off from the server, so we don't have the drift occurring. That would inevitably happen if the server only sent an update once. So we can implement a system like this. But it's important to make sure that we architect this system in a scalable way, because you'll very quickly find that you may need more than one timer at a time. It happens all the time. Let's say you've got a game. It doesn't have to be a shooter game, but let's say that your shooter game has a HUD that we're going to call game HUD, and that game has a match timer. And during the match, that timer is counting down. Well, there might be other timers in the game as well. Maybe it's a battle royale and there's a shrinking storm, and that storm shrinks every so often, running on its own timer. So that timer has to update independently of the match timer. Or let's say you're playing a zone capture game where there are multiple zones and your team has to occupy a zone for a specific amount of time before that zone changes. So there might be a timer going on for that. So because games might need multiple timers, we need to account for that when deciding how to build this system. So one way we might accomplish this is by keeping a game mode which has its own functions for starting and stopping timers. Let's say we have a class or a struct that we pass in to these functions, informing it to go ahead and start that specific timer. Now we need to inform the clients when a timer starts, when it updates, when it stops, and so on. Welcome back. So in order to sync up our time to get as close approximation as we can on the client for the server's time and take account for the single trip time, I'd like to create a player controller class here in our dedicated servers module that we can inherit from in our game projects to inherit that single trip time calculation. Well we can do so by sending a RPC or remote procedure call to the server, telling the server what our current time is on the client. And the server can send that time back. And then we can do the math. We can take the round trip time. In other words, the amount of time that it took to make the round trip from client to server and back again, and we can cut that in half and use that as our single trip time approximation. So we're basically pinging the server and waiting for that response. So for that, I'm going to create a protected section with our two remote procedure calls. If you're not familiar with our PCs, it's a way to call a function on one machine and have it execute on another. And it's the way that we can get data to the server. And it's one way we can get data back from the server. To send an RPC to the server, we create a server RPC. So we can simply create a void function. And I like to prefix my rpcs with server if it's a server RPC. So we're pinging the server. So I'm going to simply call this server underscore ping and pass a float along. And this is going to be the time of request. So whenever we call server ping we're going to send the current client time. And if this is going to be an RPC it needs a U function with a specific macro. It has to say server here. And we have to decide whether this is reliable or unreliable. In our case, I want it to be reliable, so I'm going to make it a reliable RPC. Optionally, we could create a validation function which would kick the client if it failed. Some sort of check that we made. We don't need that. So server ping can get a function definition and writer is nice with rpcs. It adds the underscore implementation to our function definition, which is what we need to do for these RPC functions. There will be an internal server ping definition generated for us, but the version we have to define is going to have an underscore implementation. Now server ping will be executed on the server at which point all we need to do is call a client RPC sending this time of request right back down to the client. So if the client pings the server, the server is going to pong the client. So I'm going to make a client PC. So it's going to be void client. Underscore. And I'm going to call it pong. And it's going to send that type of request right back down to the client. So I'm going to give it a new function macro with client reliable. And we're going to go ahead and generate this definition. Well, it takes the time of request and it subtracts that from the current time when the RPC comes back down to the client, that's going to give us our round trip time so we can say const float round trip time and we can get our current time. We can get that with get world. Get time. Seconds. This gives us our current time and we're going to subtract the time of request. So let's just say time of request when we send this server ping is let's say ten just an arbitrary value. Well it's going to take single trip time seconds to reach the server. ## Accepting Player Sessions

### Parsing Options

Welcome back. Now we're able to connect to a server and we even create game sessions and player sessions, but we never actually accept those player sessions. Now, if we expand our dedicated servers module and I'm going to open the private folder, we have our UI Game Sessions folder where we have our game sessions manager, and in our Game Sessions Manager, we're handling creating and joining game sessions, as well as creating a player session for the player and the callback create player session response is where we have the Deserialized data for that HTTP response and we're deserializing it and parsing it into an FDS player session. If we click on that and F12 over on into HTTP request types, we can see that a player session has various information in it, including the IP address and port. That allows us to travel to the server process. And we also have the player ID and the player session ID. In fact, we created a function to simply get a unique ID and append it onto a string that says player. We did that in our function get unique player ID, but the player ID for a game session can really be anything, and I'd like for that player ID to actually be the username, as players will sign up to create a user for our Cognito user pool, and their username is more or less the display name that I'd like to use, and we store their username when they sign up or sign in. We do this sign up process and sign in in the portal manager. If we go to Portal Manager and our sign in response, we're saving not only the username but the email as well in the local player subsystem, which will persist as we travel from level to level for each player. ### Fast Array Serializer

Welcome back. So our lobby is working. We have a countdown and we can travel to the match. But it's missing something. Whenever a player joins our lobby, I'd like to be able to show some kind of label as each player joins, so we can know that players are joining and we're getting closer to being able to play a match. So the question is, how do we do this and how do we do it efficiently? Now we could keep an array, say call it player info, an array of let's say structs, really any type of info we want. And we could make this array replicated. But the default way that replication works for arrays in Unreal Engine is that let's say one of these elements in the array changes. Either a new element is added, an element is removed, or an element is just changed. Some of the data inside of it. Right. Well, if we change just one element of a replicated array, then that's going to trigger replication and it's going to replicate the whole array. So no matter how many elements are in the array, the entire array is replicated. And if this is a large array that's going to take up lots of bandwidth. So the question is how do we optimize this process. It would be nice if we could only replicate what has changed. So if we change a single element then replication will be triggered and we only replicate what has changed. In other words, we replicate a delta. Now there is a way to do this. There's actually a built in construct in the engine and it's called a fast array serializer. This particular construct allows us to set up arrays that are fast replicated, and all that means is that we replicate deltas or changes rather than the entire array. So we're going to create a fast array serializer for the player info in our lobby. And while our lobby may not have a whole bunch of players in it, this is still a good exercise and a good tool to know how to use because it's a more efficient way to replicate arrays. And when our lobbies do have lots of players, let's say upwards of 20. Well, we may want that fast array serializer after all. So we're going to create a fast array serializer now. So back in my project in writer, if I hit shift shift and I type fast array serializer, I can find where that file is in fact its fast array serializer dot h.
