### DynamoDB Players Table

Welcome back! So I'm logged back into my AWS console and take a look at this. There's a visual update to the management console. Looks like it's in preview so the look and feel is changing a bit. This is probably how it looks when you first created your account. So fun times they're changing their UI but everything should pretty much be the same and in this section we're concerned with saving data to the cloud and databases. Now there are different choices for the type of database you can save your information to and for our purposes for saving persistent data to a database in AWS the DynamoDB database service is perfect. DynamoDB is a NoSQL type database and NoSQL databases have specific properties. They don't have a fixed schema meaning you can add items to a database table even if those items are not already predetermined as fields in the database. So the database is dynamic. We can add a couple of properties to the database and save them and then later decide to save a new different type of property to the database and the database is dynamic. So let's go to the DynamoDB console. I'm going to go straight to DynamoDB here and to get started in DynamoDB we create a DynamoDB table. So we can click create table and the first table I'd like to create is for our players. Each player in the game once they sign up is going to get an item in this table storing information for that player such as things like their username their email and a unique identifier that we can use as the key for the table. So I'm going to call this first table players. We can optionally call it player data. Either one is fine but I'm going to call it players and when we create a table we specify the name of a partition key. This is the primary key in the table. It's a hash value and it's used to retrieve items from the table and allocate data across hosts for scalability and availability. So we choose a partition key and we use that kind of like the key in a map. It basically is a big map and we can retrieve items from the database using that partition key or primary key. Now the key has a data type you can choose binary right zero or one number or string. We typically use strings and we use some kind of unique identifier to identify each player. So we can give the name to the partition key. I'm just going to call it database ID all lowercase and optionally you can have a sort key. This is a secondary key. Usually we say that it's the second part of the primary key and it allows you to sort or search among all items sharing the same partition key. So if you plan on having multiple entries in your database with the same partition key you can differentiate between them with a sort key. Now for this table players we plan on having a unique partition key for each player so we don't need a sort key. Now under table settings we can leave it at the default settings. Most of these settings can be altered or changed after we create the DynamoDB table. You can also customize the settings but the defaults are here. So we're going to leave it all at the defaults. We're not going to add a tag and we're going to create our players table. And so here's what it looks like in DynamoDB. In the tables section we can see all the tables that we have here and we can see that the partition key is called database ID and the S is for string. And if we ever add items to this table we can always explore them with explore items. If we click on explore items we can see any and all items for any table we select. If I click on players we can see the items here. And we're retrieving items based on the scan or query items. When we say scan in DynamoDB we're talking about getting the entire database table and retrieving every single item. You can optionally query by specifying a particular property such as an attribute or the partition key and you can only get items that have that particular partition key. But scan is an operation that retrieves all the items and we don't have any items. And we can actually create an item right here. We can select create item. We can have database ID and we can give it a value for that partition key such as test partition key one for instance. And we can create the item. And now our database has one item in it with just the partition key. If we click on it we can see that this is the item and the items can have attributes. We can add a string attribute. We can give it a name. We can say email for instance. And we can create a fake email address. And if we click Save and Close we can now see that this item with this partition key has this attribute. And this is the power of NoSQL databases. They are dynamic. You can always take some database item, identify it by its partition key, and you can add attributes to that item. And this is going to be really useful when it comes to saving data from our game. Now you can remove items from directly in the console by selecting it, going to Actions, selecting Delete Items, and hitting Delete. Now our database has no items in it.
